source: Sheppert, Shen, Geissal, Riley, Riley (2026) LLMs exhibit greater diagnostic anchoring than physicians in a forced-choice vignette study, Int J Med Inform / SSRN 6187954
finding: Abstract read via Crossref (full text not read). Nine pairs of outpatient vignettes, each with an anchored version (patient suggests an unlikely diagnosis) and a control. LLMs ranked the planted anchor first far more often than residents or attendings.
numbers: Anchor ranked first: residents 17/80 (21.2%, N=20), attendings 2/20 (10.0%, N=5), eight LLMs 40/72 (55.6%). Odds ratio LLM vs residents 3.94 (95% CI 2.32-7.33); vs attendings 4.07 (2.47-7.21); both P<0.001. Anchor in top five: LLMs 97.2%, residents 67.5%, attendings 65.0%. CMH tests stratified by vignette.
quote: LLMs demonstrated greater anchoring bias than physicians in a forced-choice differential diagnosis task.
limits: Only 9 vignettes, 72 LLM responses, 25 humans; forced ranking, not free reasoning; models not named in the abstract; anchor is an inserted patient suggestion (suggestibility), not self-generated early commitment. Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 5. Direct evidence that LLMs are more suggestible to a planted wrong lead than clinicians. Supports a rule that user or context hints are never counted as evidence for a hypothesis until a discriminating check is done. Does not show early stopping.

source: Nori et al. (2025) Sequential Diagnosis with Language Models, arXiv 2506.22405 (Science 2026), appendix ablation: single vs batched mode
finding: The only ablation the paper reports for MAI-DxO is on the question-and-test mode, not on the panel roles. Asking one test or question per turn gave the same accuracy as batching, at lower cost.
numbers: MAI-DxO (o3), test set only: accuracy 83.9% in both single and batched mode; cost $3,991 single vs $5,084 batched.
limits: Test set only (56 cases). Not a component ablation. Humans used single-turn UI; models mostly batched (limit 5 questions and 3 tests).
agent_relevance: Gap 2 stays open. Suggests that one-at-a-time information gathering does not hurt and may save cost; weak support for an open-test list that is cleared stepwise.

source: Nori et al. (2025) SDBench / MAI-DxO: structure of the five variants and what was inspected
finding: The five variants are Instant Answer (vignette only), Question Only, Budgeted, Unconstrained Budget and Ensemble. All use the same panel (Hypothesis, Challenger, Stewardship, Checklist, others) with capabilities switched on or off. No variant removes the Challenger or the hypothesis tracker alone. The claim that Challenger and Hypothesis fight anchoring rests on manual reading of disagreement cases.
numbers: Unconstrained MAI-DxO 81.9% at $4,735 vs off-the-shelf o3 78.6% at $7,850. Hand-sanitizer case: baseline o3 fixated on antibiotic toxicity, wrong, $3,431; panel asked about ingestion in round 1, right, $795. Gains significant (one-sided paired permutation, 10,000 resamples, p<0.005) for all models except o3 and o4-mini, where the significant gain was in cost.
quote: off-the-shelf o3 seemed to anchor on initial impressions.
limits: Authors are Microsoft; one worked example; no role-level ablation; no independent replication. Instant Answer accuracy exists only as a figure and was not extracted as text.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 stays open: the data cannot say which role carries the gain. The strongest model (o3) gained only 3.3 points in accuracy; the benefit is larger for weaker models.

source: Nori et al. (2025) SDBench / MAI-DxO: ensembling versus a single panel
finding: Running several independent panels and aggregating beat one panel by 3.6 points at a cost close to baseline o3. This is the closest published evidence that fresh independent derivations help more than one deeper pass.
numbers: Ensemble 85.5% at $7,184; unconstrained single panel 81.9% at $4,735; baseline o3 78.6% at $7,850; significant vs baseline (p<0.005).
limits: Ensemble cost is the sum of tests across runs, duplicates removed; model inference cost ($0.15 per case) ignored. Not compared against one panel given the same total tokens.
agent_relevance: Partial evidence for gap 4: independent re-derivation plus aggregation raises accuracy; no study here tests Mamede-style structured reanalysis against it at equal tokens.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet, ICLR 2024, arXiv 2310.01798
finding: Without an oracle label, asking a model to review and fix its own answer lowers accuracy. With the oracle label the same loop looks like a big gain, which was the source of earlier positive claims. Models more often turned correct answers into wrong ones than the reverse.
numbers: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 (round 1) and 41.8 (round 2); GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1 and 74.7. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 and 89.0; CommonSenseQA 82.0 to 79.5 and 80.0; HotpotQA 49.0 to 49.0 and 43.0. GPT-4-Turbo GSM8K 91.5 to 88.0 and 90.0. GPT-3.5 kept its first GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time.
quote: LLMs cannot properly judge the correctness of their reasoning.
limits: General reasoning tasks, not diagnosis. Prompt was a generic review request; the paper does not test structured prompts that name what to check.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: strong general evidence that an unguided recheck has a negative flip rate on correct answers. A recheck should be gated (run only when a trigger such as an open discriminating test or split samples fires) and structured, not 'are you sure'.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet: multi-agent debate versus self-consistency
finding: At equal numbers of responses, simple majority voting beats multi-agent debate. The gain from debate comes from having several samples, not from the critique.
numbers: GSM8K (GPT-3.5): standard 76.7; self-consistency 82.5 at 3 responses, 85.3 at 6, 88.2 at 9; debate about 83 at both of its settings (table text garbled in extraction, exact row mapping uncertain).
limits: Math benchmark. Debate setup of Du et al. Table layout garbled in pdftotext.
agent_relevance: Gaps 3 and 4: the multi-agent challenger in MAI-DxO and Ke 2024 may be worth no more than extra independent samples. A test at equal samples is needed before adding a challenger role (4b not-to-add).

source: Johri et al. (2025) An evaluation framework for clinical use of LLMs in patient interaction tasks (CRAFT-MD), Nature Medicine; medRxiv 2023.09.12.23295399
finding: Turning static vignettes into doctor-AI and patient-AI conversations lowered diagnostic accuracy. Multi-turn questioning did not beat a single-turn statement. Summarizing the conversation back into one vignette restored accuracy for the weaker model.
numbers: 140 skin-disease vignettes, 4-choice MCQ. GPT-4 0.919 to 0.854 (adj p<0.05); GPT-3.5 0.833 to 0.724 (adj p<0.01). Physical-exam-only floor: GPT-4 0.747, GPT-3.5 0.698. Summarization: GPT-3.5 0.724 to 0.810 (p<0.001); GPT-4 0.854 to 0.856 (ns).
limits: Dermatology only, MCQ, simulated patient. Author list not checked on the page. Measures integration of conversation, not stopping time.
agent_relevance: Gap 10. Collecting more history did not help unless it was consolidated. Supports a consolidate step (restate all findings in one block) before closure; links to Laban (c11).

source: Qiu et al. (2025) Quantifying the Reasoning Abilities of LLMs on Real-world Clinical Cases (MedR-Bench), arXiv 2503.04691
finding: 1,453 case reports (656 rare-disease). Letting models ask for more examinations (free-turn) did not raise recall of the needed examinations. Models looped on repeated requests. Diagnosis improved modestly with free turns but jumped when the key information was handed over (oracle).
numbers: Recall 1-turn vs free-turn: o3-mini 38.47 to 38.22; DeepSeek-R1 43.61 to 40.67. Diagnosis accuracy 1-turn to free-turn: R1 71.79 to 76.18; o3-mini 64.99 to 67.19; Baichuan-M1 fell. Oracle: R1 89.76, others above 83. Rare vs common diagnosis: comparable. Treatment precision for rare cases fell (o3-mini 27.03 to 23.17).
limits: Published case reports (often unusual); examinations scored against what the report listed. No measure of when the model chose to stop.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 10. Failure sits in choosing what to ask, not in reasoning once data is present: missed examinations stay missed. An explicit open-test list built from the differential is a direct fit. Rare-vs-common parity weakens the idea that models are worse on common diseases.

source: Lopez, Everett, Bunning et al. (2026) Clinician input steers AI toward accurate and harmful recommendations, arXiv 2603.14158
finding: 61 NEJM case records, 21 reasoning variants of 8 models. Adding a clinician differential pulls the model toward it, whether right or wrong. Expert context raised correct-diagnosis inclusion in all 21 models; adversarial context lowered it in 14. This is anchoring on a supplied lead measured on realistic cases.
numbers: Concordance with 3 overlapping differential items 65.8% to 93.5%; next-step overlap 20.3% to 53.8%. Expert context +20.4 points mean inclusion; adversarial -5.4 points mean (14 of 21 significant). Leading-diagnosis accuracy: expert up in all 21, adversarial down in 13. Inference-time scaling cut harmful echoing by 62.7% mild, 57.9% moderate, 76.3% severe, 83.5% death-tier.
limits: Preprint. Synthetic clinician reasoning generated for the study. Part of the expert gain is echoing, not reasoning (authors say so).
agent_relevance: Gaps 3 and 6. Two-sided: hints help when right and hurt when wrong, so the scaffold cannot just ignore them; it should check them. More thinking tokens reduced harmful echo.

source: Lopez et al. (2026) Clinician input steers AI: corrigibility and susceptibility in multi-turn challenges
finding: In multi-turn diagnostic challenges the authors measure corrigibility (switch to a correct challenge when initially wrong) and susceptibility (switch to a wrong challenge when initially right). The second is a measured flip rate on correct answers after a challenger speaks. Models split into conformist and dogmatic types.
numbers: Baseline final-diagnosis accuracy 38.1% (LLaMA-3.3-70B) to 68.0% (Gemini-3-Flash high). Conformist: GPT-4o complies 100.0% vs 97.0% (wrong vs right challenge), LLaMA-3.3-70B 100.0% vs 99.6%, Qwen3-80B-Instruct 93.5% vs 74.6%. Dogmatic: Qwen3-80B-Thinking corrigibility 11.9%, susceptibility 6.6%; GPT-5 reasoning variants corrigibility 26.3-27.5%, susceptibility 5.6-7.3%. Most models updated toward truth more often than they were pulled away.
limits: Challenge is a human-style argument for one alternative, not a self-challenge. Preprint. Models with high corrigibility tended to have low resilience to adversarial arguments.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 closed in part: a challenger can harm correct answers, and the harm depends on the model (up to 100% compliance in weak models, 6-7% in GPT-5). Any challenger step must be tested for flip rate on correct answers per model.

source: Lopez et al. (2026) Clinician input steers AI: mitigation prompts
finding: Prepending an explicit statement that the clinician is not confident recovered accuracy lost to adversarial context without cancelling the benefit of expert context. A system prompt calling the user an inexperienced clinician did similar work in some models.
numbers: Adversarial inclusion vs LLM alone: GPT-5 75.5% to 65.1% (-10.4 points, p<0.001); Claude Sonnet 4.5 70.5% to 67.3% (p=0.013); Gemini 3 Flash 76.6% to 73.7% (p=0.005). With uncertainty prompt Claude adversarial inclusion 73.0%; top-1 35.9% baseline to 43.0%. For GPT-5 and Gemini all three strategies closed the gap.
limits: Three models. Benefit tracked baseline vulnerability; severe-harm echoing in the most resistant model was not reliably cut by prompting alone.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 side-evidence: an explicit confidence tag on input changes how the model weighs it. The scaffold can label every hint with its source and strength.

source: Everett et al. (2026) From tool to teammate: RCT of clinician-AI collaborative workflows for diagnosis, npj Digital Medicine (via search summary)
finding: Reported by a secondary summary only. When the AI saw the physician's assessment first it mostly agreed, even when told to reason independently. A parallel workflow (both assess, AI then compares) did best.
numbers: 70 participants (39 residents, 31 attendings); next-step recommendations overlap completely in 52% of AI-second-opinion cases vs 24% of AI-first cases; AI alone 87%, not significantly different from AI-assisted groups; AI-first time 631 vs 688 s (ns). Figures from a news summary, not checked.
limits: Not opened; numbers unverified. Treat as a lead.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 partial. Same pattern as Lopez 2026: the model anchors on what it reads first. Argues for generating the hypothesis set before showing any external suggestion.

source: Bousquet and Beltramin (2025) Letter on Ke et al.: advantages and inconveniences of a multi-agent LLM system to mitigate cognitive biases in diagnostic challenges, J Med Internet Res 27:e69742 (via search summary)
finding: The letter asks for a single-LLM comparison, notes cost grows with agents and text volume, and notes that humans scored very low (odds ratio 3.91 for the system vs humans). The Ke authors did not reply, per the journal page summary.
numbers: OR 3.91 vs humans (as quoted). Ke 2024 preprint: initial diagnosis 0% in 80 responses (cases chosen for first-answer error); 71.3% top differential after discussion (preprint) vs 76.3% best framework (published version, as quoted).
limits: Search summary only; PMC page fetch returned no letter text. Preprint and journal figures differ.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: no new data, but it confirms the missing control: multi-agent vs single model at equal tokens. Same gap as Huang 2024 on debate.

finding: No UK replication was found in one search. Found instead: Goh 2024 JAMA Netw Open trial (76.3% vs 73.7%, adjusted +1.6 points, p=0.60; GPT-4 alone +15.5 points over conventional resources) and a 2026 trial of 249 physicians in Indonesia, Kenya and the Netherlands (Rounding et al.) as described by commentary.
numbers: From snippets: 76.3 vs 73.7, p=0.60; N=249 physicians in the 2026 trial.
limits: Snippets only. A UK paper may exist but was not located.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 stays open on the UK paper. The pattern 'model alone beats model-assisted humans' repeats; humans under-use or over-defer to the model.

source: Search note: reliability of error and cognitive-factor coding (gap 7)
finding: No post-2015 audit reporting premature-closure share with interrater agreement was found. Related reliability figures from snippets: ED record reviewers agreed on medical error at ICC 0.72, adverse events 0.52, judgment quality 0.67; a primary-care Safer Dx review reported reliability 0.37 (95% CI 0.31-0.44).
numbers: ICC 0.52-0.72 (13 reviewers, ED records, 2016); 0.37 (0.31-0.44) primary care.
limits: Snippets only; neither study codes cognitive causes.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 stays open. Raters agree only moderately on whether an error occurred, so the premature-closure-is-most-common label from one coded series should be held loosely.

source: Search note: BiasMedQA follow-up (medRxiv 2025), Wang 2024 and Nguyen 2024 (gap 10)
finding: medRxiv 2025 'LLM Reasoning Does Not Protect Against Clinical Cognitive Biases' used BiasMedQA with a base prompt and a debiasing prompt on Llama-3.3-70B and Qwen3-32B; effect sizes could not be read (PDF request returned HTML, WebFetch 403). Nguyen 2024 (J Behav Exp Finance 43) found anchoring in GPT-4, Claude 2, Gemini Pro, GPT-3.5 and suggests informed prompting helps. Wang 2024 not located.
limits: Not opened. Title suggests reasoning models are not protected; unverified.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 partial. Do not cite numbers from these until opened. If the title holds, it fits Schmidgall and Lou: more reasoning tokens alone do not remove anchoring.

finding: No study was found that repeats the early-distractor order manipulation (b17) in experienced physicians or LLMs, and none that compares stopping signals (stated confidence, sample disagreement, open-test count, rival-set size) for predicting wrong early stops in diagnosis. Closest signals: Huang 2024 (self-judged correctness unreliable), Lopez 2026 (stated clinician uncertainty shifts model weighting), Nori 2025 (certainty threshold before diagnosing, not evaluated alone).
limits: Absence of evidence from a limited search (OpenAlex quota exhausted mid-run; arXiv API returned empty).
agent_relevance: Gaps 8 and 9 stay open and are testable in-house: order manipulation is cheap; compare four stop signals on a closure-prone set.
